title: Pressure-cooker chilli con carne
subtitle: Big flavour in 25 minutes from sealed lid to table
excerpt: A proper beef and kidney bean chilli cooked under pressure. The spices bloom, the meat tenderises, and the beans hold their shape, all in under half an hour at pressure.
sourceNotes: Chilli con carne has roots in Texas and northern Mexico; the version that spread into British home cooking is a simplified beef-and-bean stew, popularised by cookbook writers from the 1970s onwards. The pressure-cooker method follows the logic of many quick-cook chilli adaptations in print since the 1990s.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cool completely and freeze in airtight containers for up to 4 months. Defrost overnight in the fridge and reheat in a saucepan over medium heat, adding a little water if needed.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the batch easily, freeze half and use within 4 months.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Chilli improves overnight. Make it the day before, refrigerate, and reheat just before serving.

content.text: Pressure-cooker chilli takes about 25 minutes. It delivers the same depth as a two-hour stovetop version. Brown the beef mince in the open pot first. Then add beans and spices, seal the lid, and let the pressure do the rest. The spices bloom and everything softens into a thick stew.

Tinned kidney beans work here and hold their shape well under pressure. If you want to cook from dried beans, they need pre-soaking and a separate 30-minute pressure cook before the chilli starts, which adds time.
Serve with rice, baked potatoes, or loaded into wraps. Toppings are part of the meal, soured cream, grated cheddar, sliced spring onions, and pickled jalapeños all make it better.

Set the pressure cooker to sauté or use the open pot on the hob. Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil over high heat. Add the beef mince and cook, breaking it up with a spoon, for 5 minutes until browned. Add the onion, red pepper, and garlic; cook for 3 minutes.

Add the chilli powder, cumin, smoked paprika, and coriander. Stir for 1 minute. Add the tomato puree and stir through. Add the tinned tomatoes, kidney beans, and beef stock. Season with salt and stir everything together.

Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 20 minutes. Quick-release the pressure. Open the lid and stir, the chilli should be thick and dark. If it looks too thin, simmer in the open pot over medium heat for 5 minutes.

rows.cause: The mince and vegetables released more liquid than the recipe accounts for.
rows.fix: Set the open pot on the hob over medium heat and simmer uncovered for 5 to 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the excess liquid has reduced.

rows.cause: The spices were added without any blooming time in the pan.
rows.fix: Stir the dry spices into the hot pot for a full minute before adding any liquid, this is the bloom step that activates them. Next time, cook the spices in the fat before adding the tomatoes.

rows.cause: Tinned beans are already cooked and break down if pressure-cooked for too long.
rows.fix: Reduce the pressure-cook time to 15 minutes next time. The beans need only enough time to absorb the flavours, not to cook further.

rows.cause: Chilli powders vary significantly in heat. Some blends contain cayenne; others are mild.
rows.fix: Stir a tablespoon of soured cream or plain yoghurt into each bowl at serving. For the pot, a small pinch of sugar and more tinned tomatoes will reduce the heat level.

content.text: Chilli is one of the best make-ahead dishes in the repertoire, it is better the next day. Refrigerate for up to 4 days or freeze in portions for up to 4 months. Reheat in a saucepan with a splash of water to loosen. Serve with rice, jacket potatoes, or in wraps.

Chilli con carne arrived in British kitchens in the 1970s. By then it had been anglicised from its Mexican-American origins. It became a student and batch-cooking staple for good reason: cheap, forgiving, scalable, and better the next day. The pressure cooker removes the hour of simmering the traditional method needs.
